title: Ridge against lasso
objectives: Explain why the lasso sets coefficients to zero and when each penalty fits.

screens.title: Slide the penalty
screens.prose: About two and a half minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. Three signals have least squares coefficients 3, 1 and −0.5. Their columns are uncorrelated and scaled alike. Slide the penalty $\lambda$ and watch the ridge and lasso fits.
screens.question: At $\lambda = 1$, how many lasso coefficients are exactly zero?

hints.text: Set the slider to 1 and read the lasso bars.
Lasso moves each coefficient towards zero by $\lambda$ and stops at zero.
3 becomes 2; 1 becomes 0; −0.5 would cross zero, so it stops at 0.

feedback.correct: Two: signal 2 lands exactly on zero and signal 3 is clipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the lasso bars at height 0.

byKey.none: You read the ridge bars. Ridge shrinks by a factor and never reaches zero.
byKey.one: You zeroed −0.5 but kept 1. At $\lambda = 1$, $|1| - 1$ is 0, so it is clipped too.

explain.text: Lasso subtracts $\lambda$ from each size and clips at zero: (2, 0, 0). Ridge divides by $1 + \lambda$: (1.5, 0.5, −0.25), none of them zero.

hints.text: Lasso subtracts; ridge divides.
Lasso: $|b| - 0.5$, clipped at zero. Ridge: $b/1.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract 0.5 for the lasso, clip at zero; divide by 1.5 for ridge.

explain.text: The lasso takes the same 0.5 off every size, so the smallest goes first. Ridge takes the same third off every coefficient, so none goes.

screens.title: A sparse truth
screens.prose: Sixty days, ten candidate signals. Only three matter: true coefficients 3, −2 and 1.5. The table shows seeded lasso and ridge fits.

state.caption: Seeded run: $n = 60$, $p = 10$, true coefficients 3, −2, 1.5 and seven zeros.

screens.question: At $\alpha = 1.0$ the lasso keeps exactly the right three. What is wrong with its coefficients?

options.text: They are pulled towards zero: 2.445 against a true 3.
Nothing: once the right signals are chosen, the fit is unbiased.
options.why: The penalty still acts on the kept ones. Each is shrunk, by 0.55 to 0.96 here.

options.text: They are too large.
options.why: Compare 2.445 with 3 and −1.040 with −2: every one is smaller in size.

options.text: Ridge is better here because it keeps all ten.
options.why: Keeping seven useless signals adds variance. The point is the shrinkage of the three kept.

hints.text: Compare each fitted value with its true value.
The lasso subtracts from every coefficient it keeps.
2.445 against 3, −1.040 against −2, 0.855 against 1.5.

feedback.correct: Selection is right, sizes are biased low.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the $\alpha = 1.0$ row with the truth.

explain.text: A large $\alpha$ picks the right three but shrinks them all. A common fix is to refit least squares on the kept signals.

screens.title: Always the lasso?
screens.prose: Two of your signals are near copies, with correlation 0.98. The chart shows the extreme case, exact copies, in a seeded run. A candidate says: "Use the lasso; it always picks the right features."
screens.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: It keeps one of the pair, chosen almost by chance, and the choice can flip between samples.
Nothing: the lasso always picks the right features, even when two of them are near copies.
options.why: You trusted the lasso with a correlated group. It keeps one member and drops the rest, not the "right" one.

options.text: It keeps both, each at half the effect, because the two copies carry the same information.
options.why: That is what ridge does. The lasso charges the same for any split, so a solver often lands on one copy; any split is optimal.

options.text: It drops both, since each adds nothing once the other is in the model.
options.why: Their joint effect is large, so the lasso keeps one of them.

hints.text: Look at the lasso bars for two copies of one signal.
The L1 penalty of (2, 0) equals that of (1, 1).
With no reason to prefer a copy, the lasso keeps one, picked by small sample quirks.

feedback.correct: The lasso picks one of a correlated group, not the true one.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the penalty charges for each split.

byKey.always: That is the trap. With correlated signals the lasso keeps one at random; a new sample may keep the other.

explain.text: Within a correlated group the lasso keeps one member, chosen by noise. Its choice of features is then unstable from sample to sample.

screens.title: Units first
screens.prose: Signal 2 is a spread. You record it in basis points instead of as a fraction, so its numbers are 10,000 times larger. The fit is the same, so its coefficient is 10,000 times smaller.
screens.question: What happens to its lasso penalty $\alpha|\beta_2|$ for the same fit?

options.text: It falls 10,000-fold, so the lasso keeps signal 2 almost whatever it is worth.
It stays the same: the lasso penalty does not care about the units of a column.
options.why: The penalty is on the coefficient, and the coefficient changed with the units.

options.text: It rises 10,000-fold, so the lasso drops signal 2 however much it is worth.
options.why: Larger numbers give a smaller coefficient, so a smaller penalty.

hints.text: The penalty is on $|\beta_2|$.
Multiplying a column by 10,000 divides its coefficient by 10,000.
So $\alpha|\beta_2|$ is 10,000 times smaller for the same fit.

feedback.correct: Scale decides who survives unless you standardise first.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the coefficient as the units change.

explain.text: Penalised fits depend on units, so standardise every column first (`stat-learning` l9-scale-first). Otherwise the choice of features follows the units, not the signal.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose:
With uncorrelated, standardised columns you saw
$$\hat\beta^{\text{lasso}} = \text{sign}(b)\max(|b| - \lambda, 0), \qquad \hat\beta^{\text{ridge}} = \frac{b}{1 + \lambda}.$$
Said aloud: "Ridge shrinks every coefficient by the same factor and never reaches zero. Lasso subtracts a fixed amount and clips at zero, so weak features drop out. Lasso picks arbitrarily within a correlated group, where ridge shares the weight."
screens.question: Which answer would you give an interviewer?

options.text: "Ridge scales coefficients down, never to zero. Lasso subtracts and clips, so it selects. In a correlated group, lasso picks one."
"Lasso is L1 and ridge is L2, so they use different norms. Both are ways to regularise a regression and stop it overfitting."
options.why: True but empty: it names the norms and says nothing about what each does to a coefficient.

options.text: "Both shrink, but ridge sets the small ones to zero. Lasso keeps every coefficient and shrinks each by the same factor."
options.why: Swapped: the lasso clips at zero; ridge never does.

options.text: "Always use lasso, because it selects features. A shorter model is easier to explain, and it is less likely to overfit."
options.why: One-sided: it ignores correlated groups, where the lasso choice is arbitrary.

feedback.correct: What each does, why lasso selects, and when each fits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that says what each penalty does to a coefficient.

explain.text: A strong answer gives the mechanism, the consequence (selection) and the case where it fails (correlated groups). Naming the norms alone is not an answer.

screens.title: Why ridge never reaches zero
screens.prose: Take uncorrelated columns with $X^\top X = nI$ and least squares coefficient $b$. Ridge minimises $\|y - X\beta\|^2 + n\lambda\|\beta\|^2$, one coordinate at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Per coordinate the loss is $n(\beta - b)^2 + n\lambda\beta^2$, plus terms free of $\beta$.
So $\beta = b/(1 + \lambda)$, zero only when $b$ is zero.
Subtract $\lambda$: $\beta = b - \lambda$, as for the lasso.
lines.why: That step comes from the slope of $|\beta|$, which is $\pm 1$. A squared penalty has slope $2\lambda\beta$, which shrinks with $\beta$.

hints.text: Write the loss for one coefficient first.
With $X^\top X = nI$ the squared error is $n(\beta - b)^2$ plus a constant.
Differentiate, set to zero, divide by $1 + \lambda$.

feedback.correct: A factor, not a subtraction: ridge never reaches zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Loss, derivative, collect, solve.

byKey.x: You borrowed the lasso step. The squared penalty pulls less as $\beta$ gets small, so it never clips.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: The ridge penalty has slope $2n\lambda\beta$, which fades near zero, so the solution is a scaled $b$. The lasso slope stays at $n\lambda$ all the way down, which is why it can stop at zero.

screens.title: Two hundred signals
screens.prose: You have 500 days and 200 candidate signals. Most are useless. Many come in families: momentum at five horizons, value on three measures. The portfolio manager wants a short list.
screens.question: Which penalty would you propose, and why?

options.text: An elastic net: the L1 part gives a short list; the L2 part keeps families together.
Ridge, since it handles correlation and keeps each family of signals together.
options.why: Ridge keeps all 200, so there is no short list.

options.text: Lasso, since it gives the shortest list and the manager wants a short list.
options.why: Within each family it keeps one horizon by chance, so the list changes from sample to sample.

options.text: Plain least squares on all 200, so that no penalty biases any coefficient.
options.why: Two hundred coefficients from 500 noisy days overfit badly.

hints.text: You need zeros and stability within families.
Lasso gives zeros; ridge shares weight in a group.
An elastic net adds both penalties.

feedback.correct: Selection from L1, grouping from L2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask for a short list that does not flip within a family.

explain.text: The elastic net combines both penalties. It drops useless signals and tends to keep or drop a correlated family together. Choose both strengths by walk-forward validation.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "What if two signals are the same signal measured twice?" The total effect is 2. Fill in what each penalty charges for two ways to split it.
screens.question: Fill in the penalty of each split.

hints.text: Both splits give the same fit, so only the penalty differs.
L1: 2 and 2. L2: 2 and 4.

feedback.correct: L1 is indifferent; L2 prefers the even split.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the sizes for L1 and the squares for L2.

explain.text: Ridge pays 2 for the even split and 4 for the lopsided one, so it splits: 0.9974 each. Lasso pays 2 either way, so it lands on a corner: 1.9455 and 0.

ideas: Ridge divides each coefficient by $1 + \lambda$ and never reaches zero.
Lasso subtracts $\lambda$ and clips at zero, so it selects, and shrinks what it keeps.
Lasso picks one member of a correlated group by chance; ridge shares, and an elastic net does both.

formula.name: Soft threshold
formula.note: With $X^\top X = nI$; ridge with $\alpha = n\lambda$ gives $b/(1 + \lambda)$.

summary.trap: The lasso does not always choose the right features: within a correlated group its choice is arbitrary.

quiz.question: What is the sum of the lasso coefficients?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract 0.5 from each size and clip at zero.

byKey.no-clip: You took 0.5 off −0.4 and got −0.9 instead of clipping at 0.
byKey.ridge: You divided by 1.5, which is ridge.

explain.text: 1.5 becomes 1.0, −0.4 is clipped to 0 and 0.9 becomes 0.4. Their sum is 1.4.

quiz.question: What is the ridge coefficient on the second column?

byKey.lasso: That is the lasso answer. Ridge never reaches zero.

explain.text: Ridge scales every coefficient by $1/(1 + \lambda) = 2/3$. So $-0.4$ becomes $-0.2667$.

quiz.prose: Five momentum signals at different horizons are highly correlated. You fit a lasso twice, on two halves of the data.
quiz.question: What do you expect?

options.text: Each half keeps one or two of the five, and not the same ones.
Both halves keep the same horizon, the one with the true effect.
options.why: Within a correlated group the choice is driven by noise, so it can change.

options.text: Both keep all five, each with an equal share of the weight.
options.why: Equal weights are what ridge gives. The lasso is indifferent to the split.

options.text: Both drop all five.
options.why: Their shared effect is real, so the lasso keeps at least one.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what the lasso does with near copies.

explain.text: The lasso keeps one or two members of a correlated group, chosen by small quirks in the sample. A different half can choose differently.

quiz.prose: You fit a lasso on raw columns: one in pounds, one in pence.
quiz.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Standardise each column, so the penalty treats them alike.
Nothing: units do not change the lasso, so fit it as it is.
options.why: The penalty is on the coefficients, and they change with the units.

options.text: Switch to ridge, which ignores units and needs no scaling.
options.why: Ridge depends on units in the same way.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the penalty is measured in.

explain.text: Both penalties act on coefficient sizes, which depend on units. Standardising puts every column on the same footing.
